propositions.text: In June 1889, Commissioner O'Reilly and surveyor Green laid out 29 Indian reserves including IR 15 for Ahousaht First Nation.
propositions.quote: In June 1889, Commissioner Peter O’Reilly (O’Reilly) of the Joint Indian Reserve Commission (JIRC) set off by boat from the port of San Juan on the west coast of Vancouver Island northwest to the Clayoquot Sound area on a week-long trip during which he, with the assistance of Commission surveyor Ashdown Green (Green), laid out 29 Indian reserves. Some of these were for the applicant Ahousaht First Nation (Ahousaht). One, no. 15, was called Marktosis, and is located on the southeast shore of Flores Island.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that in June 1889, O'Reilly and Green laid out 29 reserves including IR 15 for Ahousaht First Nation.

propositions.text: IR 15 was laid out on June 22, 1889, with boundaries defined by O'Reilly in Minutes of Decision dated June 24, 1889.
propositions.quote: IR 15 was laid out on June 22, 1889, a day that started out with heavy rain, but during which O’Reilly and Green laid out several reserves. Later, O’Reilly composed Minutes of Decision dated June 24, 1889 in which he defined the area of IR 15 as follows: Mark to sis, a reserve of two hundred and thirty (230) acres, situated on the southeast coast of Flores Island, Clayoquot Sound, and at the head of Matilda creek. Commencing at a Spruce tree, marked Indian Reserve, and running West sixty (60) chains, thence North eighty (80) chains, thence East to the seacoast, and thence following the shore in a southerly direction to the place of commencement.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IR 15 was laid out on June 22, 1889, with boundaries defined by O'Reilly in Minutes of Decision dated June 24, 1889.

propositions.text: A rough sketch of the reserve was made contemporaneously by Green.
propositions.quote: A rough sketch of the reserve made contemporaneously by Green looked like this:

paragraphs.summary: The court notes a rough sketch of the reserve was made contemporaneously by Green.

propositions.text: The sketch shows the starting point as a spruce tree marked 'Indian Reserve', graves marked by 'x', Matilda creek, a village indicated by dots, and a church at an 'x' in the village.
propositions.quote: The bold word “Spruce” indicates the starting point for measuring the boundary of the reserve. This spruce, which was marked “Indian Reserve”, is also referred to as the Commissioner’s Tree. The two “x” marks near the Commissioner’s Tree indicate graves, as noted by the word appearing adjacent thereto. The word on the left side of the sketch is “Matilda”, indicating the name of the creek that enters the reserve. The series of dots on the thin piece of land indicates the village, and the word adjacent thereto is “church”, which was located at the “x” in the village.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the sketch showing the spruce tree as starting point, graves, Matilda creek, village, and church.

propositions.text: A more precise map prepared four years later showed the reserve area shaded in pink with brown marks indicating elevation change.
propositions.quote: A more precise map prepared four years later as part of the formal survey of IR 15 (see below) showed the area of the reserve shaded in pink. The brown marks indicate elevation change.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a more precise map prepared four years later showed the reserve area shaded in pink with elevation changes.

propositions.text: The dispute concerns Lot 363, about 140 acres south of IR 15, originally part of Ahousaht land but not included in IR 15.
propositions.quote: The dispute in this appeal concerns an area to the south of IR 15 originally known as aauuknuk and later called Lot 363. This is an area of about 140 acres to the south of, and contiguous with, the southern boundary of IR 15, which includes the lake shown in the map above. There is no dispute today that Lot 363 was part of the Ahousaht’s land when the reserve was defined. However, there was doubt about this for many years. Lot 363 was not included in IR 15.

propositions.text: Lot 363 was provincial Crown land until 1904, then purchased by Presbyterian Church, later transferred to United Church, sold to private owners, and acquired by Weyerhaeuser by 2000.
propositions.quote: It was provincial Crown land until 1904 when it was purchased by the Board of Trustees of the Presbyterian Church of Canada for use as a mission and school site. In 1953, title in Lot 363 was transferred to the United Church, which then sold off portions to a series of private owners. By 1995, MacMillan Bloedel, which was later acquired by Weyerhaeuser Company Limited (Weyerhaeuser), owned a portion of Lot 363. It acquired the remaining portion in 2000.

propositions.text: In 2009, Lot 363 was set aside as an addition to IR 15, apparently with Weyerhaeuser's consent.
propositions.quote: In 2009, Lot 363 was set aside as an addition to IR 15, apparently with the consent of Weyerhaeuser.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the dispute concerns Lot 363, originally Ahousaht land but excluded from IR 15, later owned by churches and private owners, added to IR 15 in 2009.

propositions.text: In 2002, Ahousaht submitted a specific claim alleging Canada breached fiduciary duty in creating IR 15; the Minister rejected it in 2009 though Lot 363 was added to IR 15.
propositions.quote: In 2002, the Ahousaht submitted a specific claim to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (the Minister) alleging that Canada, through O’Reilly’s actions, breached its fiduciary duty and duty of care to the Ahousaht in connection with the creation of IR 15. The Minister rejected this claim in 2009, though as indicated above, Lot 363 was added to IR 15.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ahousaht submitted a claim in 2002 alleging fiduciary breach; the Minister rejected it in 2009 though Lot 363 was added to IR 15.

propositions.text: Ahousaht filed a Declaration of Claim with the Specific Claims Tribunal in 2012 alleging breach of legal obligation for not including Lot 363 in IR 15 originally and failing to correct it.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s rejection prompted the Ahousaht to file a Declaration of Claim with the Specific Claims Tribunal (SCT) in 2012. The primary ground for this Claim was paragraph 14(1)(c) of the Specific Claims Tribunal Act, S.C. 2008, c. 22, which provides for compensation to a First Nation for “a breach of a legal obligation arising from the Crown’s provision or non-provision of reserve lands.” The Ahousaht argued that the Crown breached its legal obligation to them by failing to include Lot 363 as part of IR 15 when the reserve was originally laid out, and in failing to correct the error for as long as it did thereafter. The proceeding before the SCT resulted in the decision that has led to the present application for judicial review: 2019 SCTC 1, per Chairperson Harry Slade (the Decision).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Ahousaht filed a claim in 2012 alleging breach of legal obligation for excluding Lot 363, leading to the SCT decision under review.

propositions.text: SCT found O’Reilly did not breach fiduciary duty or duty of care in creating IR 15.
propositions.quote: The SCT found that O’Reilly’s actions in connection with the creation of IR 15 did not breach Canada’s fiduciary duty and duty of care to the Ahousaht.

propositions.text: SCT recognized Ahousaht routinely used Lot 363 and such uses were cognizable.
propositions.quote: The SCT recognized that the Ahousaht routinely used Lot 363 at the time IR 15 was created, and that such uses were “cognizable”.

propositions.text: SCT concluded O’Reilly did not know of Ahousaht’s interest in Lot 363 despite ordinary diligence.
propositions.quote: However, the SCT concluded that O’Reilly did not know of the Ahousaht’s interest in Lot 363 when IR 15 was created, despite having acted with ordinary diligence in his efforts to accurately ascertain the Ahousaht’s “habits, wants and pursuits.”

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found O’Reilly did not breach fiduciary duty, recognized Ahousaht used Lot 363, but O’Reilly did not know of their interest despite diligence.

propositions.text: JIRC established in 1876 to address Indian land in BC; Commissioners to fix reserves after full enquiry.
propositions.quote: The JIRC under which O’Reilly worked was established in 1876, with the approval of Canada and British Columbia, to address the question of Indian land in British Columbia. Commissioners like O’Reilly were tasked to “visit … each Indian Nation … in British Columbia and after full enquiry on the spot, into all matters affecting the question, to fix and determine for each Nation separately the number, extent and locality of the Reserve or Reserves to be allowed to it.”

propositions.text: Commissioners instructed to be guided by spirit of Union terms, pursuing a liberal policy and considering habits, wants and pursuits of each Nation.
propositions.quote: Commissioners were also instructed to: […] be guided generally by the spirit of the terms of Union between the Dominion and the Local Governments, which contemplates a “liberal policy” being pursued towards the Indians; and in the case of each particular Nation regard shall be had to the habits, wants and pursuits of such Nation.

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found JIRC was established in 1876 to fix reserves after enquiry, guided by a liberal policy considering each Nation's habits and wants.

propositions.text: Article 13 of Terms of Union assigned Indian land management to Dominion Government with a liberal policy continuing BC's practice.
propositions.quote: Article 13 of the Terms of Union referred to in the above-quoted passage stated: The charge of the Indians, and the trusteeship and management of the lands reserved for their use and benefit, shall be assumed by the Dominion Government, and a policy as liberal as that hitherto pursued by the British Columbia Government shall be continued by the Dominion Government after the Union.

propositions.text: Land tracts to be conveyed by Local Government to Dominion Government in trust for Indians; disagreements referred to Secretary of State for the Colonies.
propositions.quote: To carry out such policy, tracts of land of such extent as it has hitherto been the practice of the British Columbia Government to appropriate for that purpose, shall from time to time be conveyed by the Local Government to the Dominion Government in trust for the use and benefit of the Indians on application of the Dominion Government; and in case of disagreement between the two Governments respecting the quantity of such tracts of land to be so granted, the matter shall be referred for the decision of the Secretary of State for the Colonies.

paragraphs.summary: The SCT noted Article 13 assigned Indian land management to Dominion Government with a liberal policy and land conveyance procedures.

propositions.text: Williams Lake SCC ruled Crown's fiduciary duty in land interests is grounded in cognizable land interests.
propositions.quote: In Williams Lake Indian Band v. Canada (Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development), 2018 SCC 4, [2018] 1 S.C.R. 83 at para. 80 (Williams Lake), the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that the Crown’s fiduciary duty in interests in land is grounded in land “capable of being known or recognized”, i.e. cognizable.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Williams Lake SCC ruling that Crown's fiduciary duty in land is grounded in cognizable interests.

propositions.text: SCT stated Crown’s fiduciary duty requires loyalty, good faith, full disclosure, and ordinary diligence for beneficiaries' best interests.
propositions.quote: At paragraph 43 of the Decision, the SCT considered that the Crown’s fiduciary duty is “to act with respect to the interest of the aboriginal peoples with loyalty, good faith, full disclosure appropriate to the subject matter and with ‘ordinary’ diligence in what it reasonably regard[s] as the best interest of the beneficiaries” (citing Williams Lake at para. 55).

propositions.text: SCT stated ordinary diligence requires adequate inquiry into beneficiary’s land interests.
propositions.quote: The SCT went on at paragraph 49 to state that ordinary diligence “imposes a standard of conduct on the Crown in its dealings with a beneficiary, thus requiring adequate inquiry by the Crown into the affected beneficiary’s interests in land.”

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found Crown’s fiduciary duty requires loyalty, good faith, full disclosure, and ordinary diligence including adequate inquiry into land interests.

propositions.text: The question is whether O’Reilly knew or would have known of Ahousaht’s interest in Lot 363 with ordinary diligence, not whether the interest was cognizable.
propositions.quote: As stated at paragraph 51 of the Decision, “the question in the present matter is not whether the Ahousaht had a cognizable interest, but whether it was apparent to Commissioner O’Reilly or, if acting with ordinary diligence, would have been apparent to Commissioner O’Reilly.”

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found the issue is whether O’Reilly knew or would have known of Ahousaht’s interest in Lot 363 with ordinary diligence.

propositions.text: O’Reilly was instructed to maintain friendly relations, interfere little with tribal arrangements, and avoid disturbing Indians in possession of villages, fishing stations, and burial places.
propositions.quote: The SCT looked at the instructions that were given to O’Reilly concerning his work. Among other things, he was told the following upon receiving his Commission in 1880: The Government considers it of paramount importance that in the settlement of the land question, nothing should be done to militate against the maintenance of friendly relations between the Government and the Indians, you should therefore interfere as little as possible with any tribal arrangements being specially careful not to disturb the Indians in the possession of any villages, fur trading posts, settlements, clearings, burial places and fishing stations occupied by them and to which they may be specially attached.

propositions.text: O’Reilly was instructed to clearly define fishing stations, explain to Indians, avoid violent changes in habits, and encourage legitimate pursuits.
propositions.quote: Their fishing stations should be very clearly defined by you in your reports to the Dept. and distinctly explained to the Indians interested therein so as to avoid further future misunderstanding on this most important point. You should in making allotments of lands for reserves make no attempt to cause any violent or sudden change in the habits of the Indian Band for which you may be setting apart the Reserve land; or to divert the Indians from any legitimate pursuits or occupations which they may be profitably following or engaged in; you should on the contrary encourage them in any branch of industry in which you find them so engaged.

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found O’Reilly was instructed to maintain friendly relations, avoid disturbing Indians' possessions, clearly define fishing stations, and encourage legitimate pursuits.

propositions.text: SCT reproduced 1878 report by Commissioner Sproat emphasizing importance of leaving Indians in old places, understanding customs, and obtaining consent for reserve assignments.
propositions.quote: These same instructions also referred to an 1878 report of the previous Commissioner, G.M Sproat, which report contained further guidance. The SCT reproduced the following extracts therefrom at paragraph 119 of the Decision: The first requirement is to leave the Indians in the old places to which they are attached. The people here so cling at present to these places that no advantage coming to them from residence elsewhere would reconcile them to the change.… The British Columbian Indian thinks, in his way and in a degree, as much of a particular rock from which his family has caught fish from time immemorial as an Englishman thinks of the home that has come to him from his forefathers. This strong feeling which is well known, but the force of which I did not, until this year, fully appreciate, cannot be justly or safely disregarded. … …I am sorry, as a matter of historical truth, to have to say that the facts disclosed in several of my Field Minutes forwarded from different places are inconsistent with the fair and reasonable attention to Indian business which might have been expected from the British Columbia government in pre-confederation days, and which was enjoined upon the colonial authorities in repeated dispatches from the Home government. … It is almost unnecessary to say that the manners and customs of the native population must be understood before land reserves can be satisfactorily assigned for their use…. None of the rulers of British Columbia since Sir James Douglas left office seem to have appreciated this fact.… … I have solved several apparently insoluble problems this year by discovering, that what the Indians really wanted was not so much good ploughland, as some old “places of fun” up in the mountains or some place of fishing-resort where, at certain seasons, they assemble to fish, dig roots and race their horses.… … As a sample of what I mean by too “summary” procedure, I may mention that, in assigning a compact reserve in a district, proper arrangements do not, in all cases, seem to have been made to obtain the intelligent consent of the Indians to the change…

paragraphs.summary: The SCT reproduced 1878 report emphasizing leaving Indians in old places, understanding customs, and obtaining consent for reserve assignments.

propositions.text: SCT noted instructions to surveyors to point out reserve boundaries to chiefs and head men to hear objections.
propositions.quote: The SCT also noted instructions to field surveyors involved in setting reserves (like Green) to point out, on the ground, the boundaries of the reserve to the chief and head men in order to permit the Commissioner to hear any objections.

paragraphs.summary: The SCT noted surveyors were instructed to show reserve boundaries to chiefs and head men to hear objections.

propositions.text: SCT defined Crown’s fiduciary duty as acting with loyalty, good faith, full disclosure, and ordinary diligence in beneficiaries' best interests before acquiring legal interest in land.
propositions.quote: Citing Williams Lake at para. 55 and Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada, 2002 SCC 79, [2002] 4 S.C.R. 245 at para. 97, the SCT defined the fiduciary duty on O’Reilly as follows: […] Prior to the acquisition of a “legal interest” in land that is subject to the reserve creation process, the Crown’s sui generis fiduciary duty is “to act with respect to the interest of the aboriginal peoples with loyalty, good faith, full disclosure appropriate to the subject matter and with ‘ordinary’ diligence in what it reasonably regard[s] as the best interest of the beneficiaries” […]

paragraphs.summary: The SCT defined Crown’s fiduciary duty as acting with loyalty, good faith, full disclosure, and ordinary diligence before acquiring legal interest in land.

propositions.text: O’Reilly wrote in 1890 he had a long conversation with the Chief and many people on June 19, 1889, discussing reserve locations and inviting them to accompany him.
propositions.quote: The SCT noted that O’Reilly had indicated (in a letter to the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs (SGIA) dated March 5, 1890) that he had a long conversation with the “Chief” and many of his people in June 19, 1889. They discussed where the reserves should be situated, and O’Reilly invited them to accompany him to the relevant locations, either on his steamer or being towed in their canoes. He indicated that they gladly accepted.

propositions.text: It is unclear if the Chief was Noukamis, but O’Reilly’s diary shows he chatted with Chief Noukamis on June 22, 1889.
propositions.quote: It is not clear whether the Chief identified here was Noukamis, then Chief of the Ahousaht. However, O’Reilly’s diary indicates that on the day that he defined the boundaries of IR 15 (June 22, 1889) he had a long chat with Chief Noukamis.

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found O’Reilly had a long conversation with the Chief and people in June 1889, possibly Chief Noukamis, on reserve locations.

propositions.text: SCT found Chief Noukamis was present when O’Reilly and Green visited Marktosis village, based on his awareness of fishing stations and need for input on southern boundary near burial sites.
propositions.quote: The SCT also found that Chief Noukamis was present when O’Reilly and Green visited the Marktosis village. This finding was based on two things. First, Chief Noukamis was aware of the importance to his people of securing their fishing stations and villages, and of his responsibility to ensure that this was done (see paragraph 181 of the Decision). Second, locating the southern boundary of IR 15 just south of burial sites located in a forested area would have required input from the Ahousaht (see paragraph 167 of the Decision).

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found Chief Noukamis was present when O’Reilly and Green visited Marktosis village, based on his awareness and boundary input needs.

propositions.text: SCT found unclear how southern boundary starting point was chosen, set further south than village limit
propositions.quote: The SCT found that it was not clear how the starting point for the southern boundary of the reserve, the Commissioner’s Tree, was chosen. It was not set at one obvious point, the outer limit of the village. It was set further south.

propositions.text: SCT found no evidence of distinction between forested land north and south of boundary
propositions.quote: The SCT found that there was no evidence for any distinction between the forested land just north and just south of the southern boundary

propositions.text: SCT concluded boundary set based on consultation with Chief Noukamis
propositions.quote: and concluded that it must have been set based on consultation with Chief Noukamis.

propositions.text: SCT found boundary location south of burial sites showed O’Reilly was sensitive to including them and inquired about their location
propositions.quote: The SCT also found that the location of the southern boundary just south of burial sites indicated that O’Reilly was sensitive to the need to include them in the reserve and inquired as to their location

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found unclear boundary choice, no land distinction, boundary set with Chief Noukamis, and O’Reilly included burial sites sensitively.

propositions.text: SCT concluded O’Reilly and Green likely unaware of lake on Lot 363 near southern boundary
propositions.quote: the SCT concluded that O’Reilly and Green were likely not aware of it.

propositions.text: SCT noted lake was in forested area, separated by elevated land, and it was raining heavily when reserve laid out
propositions.quote: The SCT noted that (i) it was in a forested area, (ii) there was an area of elevated land between the lake and the Commissioner’s Tree, and (iii) it was raining heavily the day the reserve was laid out

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found O’Reilly and Green likely unaware of lake due to forest, elevation, and heavy rain.

propositions.text: SCT found no evidence O’Reilly was told of Lot 363's value
propositions.quote: The SCT also noted that there was no evidence that O’Reilly was told of the value of Lot 363

propositions.text: SCT concluded absence of notes on fishery, timber or other values implied O’Reilly was not informed
propositions.quote: The SCT concluded that the absence of notes by O’Reilly attributing fishery, timber or other values to Lot 363 strongly implied that O’Reilly was not informed of them

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found no evidence O’Reilly knew Lot 363's value and absence of notes implied he was uninformed.

propositions.text: SCT aware Ahousaht were canoe builders and valued timber on Lot 363 by oral history
propositions.quote: The SCT was aware that the Ahousaht were canoe builders. It also noted oral history that the Ahousaht attributed value to the timbered land on Lot 363.

propositions.text: SCT concluded timber value was not for canoe construction
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, the SCT concluded that any value such timber may have had was not for the construction of canoes

paragraphs.summary: The SCT noted Ahousaht were canoe builders and valued timber, but timber was not for canoes.

propositions.text: O’Reilly's 1890 letter described IR 15 with 230 acres, village details, and land of small value
propositions.quote: In his March 5, 1890 letter to the SGIA, O’Reilly described IR 15 as follows: No15. Mark-to-sis, contains two hundred, and thirty (230) acres... The land is rocky, and of small value; a few potato patches at the rear of the village...

paragraphs.summary: O’Reilly's 1890 letter described IR 15's size, village, and land as rocky and of small value.

propositions.text: SCT concluded O’Reilly exercised ordinary diligence and made adequate inquiry but was uninformed of Lot 363's value
propositions.quote: The SCT concluded that the evidence did not establish that O’Reilly failed to exercise ordinary diligence. He made adequate inquiry, but was not informed of the particular value attributed to Lot 363

paragraphs.summary: The SCT found O’Reilly exercised diligence but was not informed of Lot 363's value.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue SCT erred in finding O’Reilly met standard of care excluding Lot 363 from IR 15
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht argue that the SCT erred in finding that O’Reilly met the requisite standard of care when he failed to include Lot 363 within IR 15.

paragraphs.summary: Ahousaht argue SCT erred finding O’Reilly met care standard excluding Lot 363.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue denial of procedural fairness when Justice Whelan recused and Chairperson Slade replaced him
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht also argue that they were denied procedural fairness when the judge who was expected to hear their claim before the SCT, Justice Larry Whelan, recused himself and was replaced by Chairperson Slade.

paragraphs.summary: Ahousaht argue procedural fairness denied by judge replacement before SCT.

propositions.text: SCT intervened with submissions on procedural fairness issue
propositions.quote: The SCT itself makes submissions as an intervener on the issue of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The SCT intervened with submissions on procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Two issues identified will be addressed, starting with procedural fairness
propositions.quote: The two issues identified above are addressed in the paragraphs below, starting with the issue of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: Court will address two issues, starting with procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness, per Mission Institution v. Khela and Vidéotron
propositions.quote: The standard of review on issues of procedural fairness is essentially correctness: Mission Institution v. Khela... Vidéotron Ltée v. Canada (Shared Services)...

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness, per precedent.

propositions.text: Justice Whelan conducted claim before SCT for almost five years from June 2013 to June 2018
propositions.quote: Justice Whelan had conduct of the claim before the SCT for almost five years from June 2013 to June 2018.

propositions.text: Justice Whelan presided over case management, oral history hearing, expert evidence hearing, site visit, and mediation
propositions.quote: During this time, he: A. Presided over numerous case management conferences; B. Presided over an oral history hearing... C. Attended a site visit... D. Conducted a mediation...

paragraphs.summary: Justice Whelan conducted claim for five years, presiding over hearings, site visit, and mediation.

propositions.text: Mediation failed to settle claim; Validity Hearing scheduled for July 12-13, 2018
propositions.quote: As the mediation did not succeed in settling the Ahousaht’s claim, a hearing to argue the validity of the claim (Validity Hearing) was scheduled for July 12 and 13, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Mediation failed; Validity Hearing scheduled for July 2018.

propositions.text: Parties agreed Justice Whelan would act as mediator and hear opening statements, then share impressions
propositions.quote: In that agreement, the parties requested that Justice Whelan... act as the mediator. The Mediation Agreement contemplated that... he would hear the parties’ respective opening statements and arguments, and then share his impressions

paragraphs.summary: Parties agreed Justice Whelan would mediate and share impressions after opening statements.

propositions.text: Parties agreed Justice Whelan would preside over Validity Hearing if mediation failed
propositions.quote: The parties also agreed that, if the mediation did not resolve the matter... Justice Whelan should preside over the Validity Hearing

propositions.text: Parties waived requirement that person who hears must decide, allowing replacement judge if needed
propositions.quote: They agreed to waive the requirement that the person who hears must decide...

propositions.text: Mediation Agreement allowed another SCT member to preside if Justice Whelan unavailable
propositions.quote: should Justice Whelan... be unavailable... another member of the SCT... may preside over the Validity Hearing in his place

propositions.text: Parties agreed mediation did not prejudice or breach procedural fairness rights
propositions.quote: the parties agreed that the mediation as contemplated did not prejudice them or breach their right to procedural fairness

paragraphs.summary: Parties agreed Whelan would preside if mediation failed, waived hearing-decides rule, allowed replacement, and agreed mediation was fair.

propositions.text: After mediation, Justice Whelan felt inappropriate to preside over Validity Hearing due to mediation involvement
propositions.quote: Justice Whelan indicated... he felt it would be inappropriate for him to preside over the Validity Hearing and decide the matter.

propositions.text: Chairperson Slade replaced Justice Whelan and advised parties by Direction dated June 21, 2018
propositions.quote: Chairperson Slade then took over this role and advised the parties by Direction dated June 21, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Whelan recused due to mediation role; Chairperson Slade replaced him and notified parties.

propositions.text: Ahousaht concerned about late replacement of familiar judge by new judge
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht expressed concern with the late replacement of the judge who had become familiar with the matter over several years by a judge with no prior involvement with the matter.

propositions.text: Ahousaht noted parties' agreement that Justice Whelan could continue despite unsuccessful mediation
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht noted the express agreement of the parties that Justice Whelan could continue even if the mediation were unsuccessful.

propositions.text: Chairperson Slade convened case management conference, considered concerns, agreed Whelan should not continue
propositions.quote: Chairperson Slade convened a case management conference to discuss how to proceed... he indicated that he agreed with Justice Whelan that it would be inappropriate for the latter to continue

paragraphs.summary: Ahousaht concerned about judge replacement; Chairperson Slade agreed Whelan should not continue.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue SCT should have addressed procedural unfairness by letting Whelan continue or re-hearing evidence
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht argue that Justice Whelan’s late withdrawal and replacement created a procedural unfairness that the SCT should have addressed in one of two ways...

paragraphs.summary: Ahousaht argue SCT should have addressed procedural unfairness by Whelan continuing or re-hearing evidence.

propositions.text: Ahousaht did not raise procedural fairness concerns before SCT at earliest opportunity
propositions.quote: I note first that the Ahousaht have pointed to nothing to indicate that they expressed any concerns before the SCT that the late replacement of the hearing judge would give rise to procedural unfairness.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness allegations must be raised at earliest practical opportunity
propositions.quote: The jurisprudence is well settled that an allegation of a violation of procedural fairness must be raised at the earliest practical opportunity

propositions.text: Ahousaht's concerns before Chairperson Slade were about efficiency, not procedural fairness
propositions.quote: The concerns they expressed before Chairperson Slade about the replacement of Justice Whelan appear to have been more with regard to the efficiency of the process. They did not mention procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Ahousaht failed to explicitly state procedural fairness concerns when discussing other concerns
propositions.quote: If the Ahousaht had concerns about procedural fairness, they should have stated them explicitly when their other concerns were discussed.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Ahousaht failed to raise procedural fairness concerns early and explicitly.

propositions.text: No indication Ahousaht proposed re-hearing evidence approach to Chairperson Slade
propositions.quote: I see no indication that the Ahousaht ever proposed such an approach.

propositions.text: Difficult to fault Chairperson Slade for not re-hearing evidence when Ahousaht did not raise it
propositions.quote: It would be difficult to fault Chairperson Slade for not having adopted that approach when the Ahousaht themselves did not raise it.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no fault with Chairperson Slade for not re-hearing evidence as Ahousaht did not request it.

propositions.text: It would have been inappropriate for Justice Whelan to preside over the Validity Hearing given his concerns about signalling views on the merits.
propositions.quote: it would have been inappropriate for Justice Whelan to preside over the Validity Hearing and decide the matter despite his concern about possibly having signalled his views on the merits.

propositions.text: It would have been inappropriate and impractical for Chairperson Slade to push Justice Whelan to ignore his misgivings.
propositions.quote: It would have been inappropriate for Chairperson Slade to push Justice Whelan to ignore his misgivings. Doing so would likely also have been impractical; it would amount to asking a judge to do something that he considers unethical.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it inappropriate for Justice Whelan to preside given his concerns and that Chairperson Slade should not have pushed him to ignore misgivings.

propositions.text: There was no unfairness in how the Validity Hearing was conducted and decided.
propositions.quote: I see nothing unfair in how the Validity Hearing was conducted and decided.

propositions.text: The parties contemplated that Justice Whelan might not continue if mediation failed, as per the Mediation Agreement.
propositions.quote: The parties indicated clearly in the Mediation Agreement that they contemplated the possibility that Justice Whelan would not be able to continue in the matter if the mediation were unsuccessful.

propositions.text: The parties waived the requirement that the person who hears must decide, accepting another judge might decide after Justice Whelan.
propositions.quote: the parties’ waiver of the requirement that the person who hears must decide suggests that they accepted the possibility that another judge might consider the evidence that had been heard by Justice Whelan.

propositions.text: Paragraph 16 of the Mediation Agreement allows another SCT member to preside if Justice Whelan is unavailable.
propositions.quote: [s]hould Justice Whelan, for any reason, be unavailable to preside over the continuation of Validity Hearing, the Parties agree that another member of the SCT, as the SCT Registry may determine, may preside over the Validity Hearing in his place.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no unfairness in the hearing, noting parties anticipated Justice Whelan might be replaced per the Mediation Agreement.

propositions.text: Ahousaht assert three errors in SCT's factual findings relevant to O'Reilly's standard of care.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht assert three errors regarding findings of fact by the SCT, each one relevant to the SCT’s conclusion that O’Reilly met the standard of care by exercising ordinary diligence and making adequate inquiries.

propositions.text: Errors concern location of Commissioner’s Tree, presence of Chief Noukamis at Marktosis, and whether O’Reilly was informed of lake on Lot 363.
propositions.quote: The alleged errors concern (i) the location of the Commissioner’s Tree delineating the southern boundary of IR 15, (ii) the presence of Chief Noukamis at Marktosis when O’Reilly and Green were there, and (iii) whether O’Reilly was informed of the presence of the lake on Lot 363.

propositions.text: The standard of review for these alleged errors is to be considered.
propositions.quote: (1) Standard of Review

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges three factual errors by SCT relevant to O'Reilly's care; the standard of review is raised.

propositions.text: The parties agree and the court concurs that the applicable standard of review is reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The parties agree, and I concur, that the standard of review applicable to the alleged errors is reasonableness: Williams Lake at para 27.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with parties that reasonableness is the applicable standard of review.

propositions.text: Vavilov sets out the reasonableness standard of review with key aspects including respectful attention to reasons, justification, transparency, burden on challenger, rationality, and refraining from reweighing evidence.
propositions.quote: The reasonableness standard of review was discussed by the Supreme Court of Canada in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov...

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes Vavilov's reasonableness standard of review principles relevant here.

propositions.text: The alleged errors concern factual inferences drawn by SCT, which were open to it and not irrational or logically fallacious.
propositions.quote: In respect of all of the alleged errors, they concern inferences of fact that were drawn by the SCT based on the evidence...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SCT's factual inferences open and reasonable despite possible alternative inferences.

propositions.text: SCT inferred the Commissioner’s Tree location was chosen after consulting Chief Noukamis to include burial sites.
propositions.quote: the SCT inferred that the Commissioner’s Tree delineating the southern boundary was chosen based on consultation with Chief Noukamis, and in order to ensure that burial sites were included in the reserve.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes SCT inferred the Commissioner’s Tree location was chosen with Chief Noukamis' consultation to include burial sites.

propositions.text: Ahousaht note later survey found more graves and burial in trees south of boundary.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht note that the formal survey of IR 15 prepared four years later noted many more grave sites than those identified by Green. The Ahousaht also note that there was evidence of people being “buried” in trees south of the southern boundary.

propositions.text: These assertions do not impair SCT's inferences; SCT was aware of burial in trees and no evidence O’Reilly knew of graves south of boundary.
propositions.quote: neither of these assertions impairs the inferences that the SCT drew from the evidence. The SCT was clearly aware of the practice of burial in trees...and there is no indication in the evidence that O’Reilly knew or should have known of any graves south of the southern boundary of IR 15.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant notes more graves and burial in trees; court finds SCT aware and no evidence O’Reilly knew of graves south of boundary.

propositions.text: The SCT's inferences about the Commissioner’s Tree selection were not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I am not convinced that the inferences the SCT drew with regard to the selection of the Commissioner’s Tree were unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court is not convinced SCT's inferences about Commissioner’s Tree selection were unreasonable.

propositions.text: SCT found Chief Noukamis was present at Marktosis with O’Reilly and Green despite lack of direct evidence.
propositions.quote: the SCT found that Chief Noukamis was present when O’Reilly and Green visited the Marktosis village...The SCT acknowledged the lack of direct evidence...but drew inferences from the evidence despite this.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue no evidence Chief Noukamis was present at Marktosis with O’Reilly and Green.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht argue that there is no evidentiary basis for this finding...it does not record that Chief Noukamis accompanied him there.

propositions.text: SCT was entitled to draw inferences despite lack of direct evidence.
propositions.quote: The SCT was entitled to do that.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues no evidence Chief Noukamis was present; court finds SCT entitled to infer presence despite lack of direct evidence.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue no reason for Chief Noukamis to travel to Marktosis, implying he was not present.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht argue that there would be no reason for Chief Noukamis to travel to Marktosis, and that the implication from the evidence is that he did not accompany O’Reilly and Green there.

propositions.text: SCT found Chief Noukamis was present due to his responsibility as chief; court not convinced this finding was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The SCT found that Chief Noukamis was present...including his responsibility as chief to be present...I am not convinced that this was an unreasonable finding...It is not the role of this Court to reweigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues no reason for Chief Noukamis to be present; court upholds SCT's reasonable finding of his presence.

propositions.text: Ahousaht question reliability of O’Reilly’s diary and letter, suggesting possible misremembering or embellishment.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht question the reliability of some of the information provided by O’Reilly...that he may have misremembered or embellished what he did.

propositions.text: Possible alternative findings do not make SCT’s findings unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the existence of such possible alternative findings do not lead to a conclusion that the SCT’s findings were unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant questions O’Reilly’s reliability; court finds possible alternatives do not render SCT’s findings unreasonable.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue O’Reilly’s invitation was seen as an adventure, not serious information gathering.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht also ask this Court to conclude that O’Reilly’s comments give the impression that his invitation...was considered...more of an adventure or a lark than a serious attempt to gather information.

propositions.text: It is not court’s task to reach such conclusions; no basis beyond speculation for applicant’s view; conflicts with SCT’s finding that Ahousaht understood reserve setting was important.
propositions.quote: it is not the task of this Court to reach such conclusions...I see no basis, other than speculation, for the conclusion...such a conclusion would conflict with the SCT’s reasonable finding that the Ahousaht understood that the setting of reserves was an important matter.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues O’Reilly’s invitation was not serious; court rejects speculation and upholds SCT’s finding of Ahousaht’s understanding.

propositions.text: SCT concluded O’Reilly and Green likely unaware of lake on Lot 363 south of IR 15 boundary.
propositions.quote: the SCT concluded that O’Reilly and Green were likely not aware of the lake located on Lot 363 just south of the southern boundary of IR 15.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue O’Reilly and Green had duty to traverse southern boundary and would have seen lake and its value.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht argue that O’Reilly and Green had a duty to traverse the southern boundary, and would have seen the lake if they had. They also argue that, had O’Reilly seen the lake, he would have understood its value to them as a source of fish, and would have included Lot 363 as part of IR 15.

paragraphs.summary: SCT found O’Reilly unaware of lake; applicant argues they had duty to traverse boundary and recognize lake’s value.

propositions.text: Applicant offers little support for duty to traverse boundary; SCT did not err in not finding fiduciary breach.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht offer little support for a duty to traverse the southern boundary, and I do not accept that the SCT erred in not finding a breach of the fiduciary duty to the Ahousaht in the failure of O’Reilly and/or Green to traverse the southern boundary of IR 15.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects applicant’s argument of duty to traverse boundary and finds no fiduciary breach by SCT.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue O’Reilly could not claim ignorance of lake after seeing formal survey map years later.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht also argue that, even if O’Reilly was unaware of the lake when he visited Marktosis, he could not have claimed ignorance of it once he saw (and signed) the formal survey prepared a few years later.

propositions.text: Court accepts O’Reilly may have seen lake on map but not convinced he had to make further inquiries or modify boundaries.
propositions.quote: I accept that O’Reilly may have seen the lake on Lot 363 on the map in the formal survey, but I am not convinced that doing so would necessarily have required him to make further inquiries with a view to modifying the boundaries of IR 15.

propositions.text: Map indication alone does not show lake or land was valuable to Ahousaht, especially given Chief Noukamis’ presence during visit.
propositions.quote: The mere indication on the map of a body of water near the border of IR 15 would not, without more, indicate that either the body of water or the land surrounding it were necessarily of value to the Ahousaht. This is especially so in view of the SCT’s reasonable finding that Chief Noukamis was present when O’Reilly visited Marktosis in order to indicate the lands the Ahousaht used.

propositions.text: SCT did not err in not including further inquiry as part of fiduciary duty.
propositions.quote: I am not convinced that the SCT erred in not including such a step as part of the fiduciary duty owed to the Ahousaht.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues O’Reilly could not ignore lake after survey; court finds no error in SCT not requiring further inquiry or boundary change.

propositions.text: Ahousaht argue evidence would have been treated differently by Justice Whelan than Chairperson Slade, including oral history and site visit.
propositions.quote: The Ahousaht make several arguments concerning evidence that would have been treated differently by Justice Whelan than by Chairperson Slade. Examples include (i) oral history concerning the suitability of timber on Lot 363 for canoes, and (ii) a visit to IR 15, which would have shown just how close the lake is to the southern boundary of IR 15.

propositions.text: SCT was aware of oral history and timber value evidence and treated it reasonably.
propositions.quote: the SCT was clearly aware of this evidence. The oral history, which was provided by Elder Louis Frank Sr., was discussed in the Decision at paragraphs 55 to 62, and the value of the timber on Lot 363 was discussed at paragraphs 171 to 175. I see nothing unreasonable in the SCT’s treatment of the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues evidence would be treated differently by Justice Whelan; court finds SCT aware and reasonable in treatment.

propositions.text: Lake is about 60 metres from southern boundary; SCT noted this.
propositions.quote: The proximity of the lake to IR 15 is clear from the evidence (the formal survey indicates that it was 3 chains – about 60 metres – from the southern boundary), and the SCT noted this at paragraph 171 of the Decision.

propositions.text: Site visit in 2018 unlikely to affect outcome or help understand 1889 visitor’s perspective.
propositions.quote: it is not clear to me how a site visit to see this proximity in person could have affected the outcome...it is not clear to me that a site visit in 2018 would have assisted Chairperson Slade to imagine what would have been apparent to a visitor in 1889.

propositions.text: SCT concluded O’Reilly and Green had not seen the lake based on distance and terrain from Commissioner’s Tree, not boundary.
propositions.quote: The SCT’s conclusion that O’Reilly and Green had not seen the lake was based on the distance and terrain from the Commissioner’s Tree, not from the southern boundary of IR 15.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes lake proximity and finds site visit unlikely to affect outcome; SCT concluded O’Reilly and Green had not seen lake.

propositions.text: No unfairness in SCT procedure or substitution of Chairperson Slade for Justice Whelan in Validity Hearing.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, I find that there was no unfairness in the procedure before the SCT, and specifically with regard to the substitution of Chairperson Slade for Justice Whelan to hear and decide the Validity Hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes no unfairness in SCT procedure or substitution of Chairperson Slade for Justice Whelan.

propositions.text: The Decision was reasonable and without error.
propositions.quote: It is also my view that the Decision was reasonable and without error.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes the Decision was reasonable and without error.

propositions.text: Dismiss the present application for judicial review with costs.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the present application for judicial review with costs.

propositions.text: Judges Locke, Laskin, and LeBlanc agree with the dismissal.
propositions.quote: “George R. Locke” J.A. “I agree. J. B. Laskin J.A.” “I agree. René LeBlanc J.A.”

propositions.text: The decision is from the Federal Court of Appeal, dated July 9, 2021, heard online March 10 and 11, 2021.
propositions.quote: FEDERAL COURT OF APPEAL ... DATED: JULY 9, 2021 ... DATE OF HEARING: March 10 and 11, 2021

propositions.text: The parties are Ahousaht First Nation (applicant) and Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada (respondent).
propositions.quote: STYLE OF CAUSE: AHOUSAHT FIRST NATION v. HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN IN RIGHT OF CANADA, AS REPRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT

propositions.text: Counsel and solicitors for applicant, respondent, and intervener are named.
propositions.quote: APPEARANCES: Stan Ashcroft For The Applicant James Rendell For The Respondent Paul J.J. Cavalluzzo Lara Koerner Yeo For The Intervener SOLICITORS OF RECORD: Ashcroft & Company ... Nathalie G. Drouin ... Cavalluzzo LLP ...

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application with costs, with agreement from all judges, and provides hearing details and parties' counsel.
